text: May 13th, 1950. An old wartime airfield in the middle of England.
The King and Queen are in the crowd:
the only time a reigning British monarch
has ever attended a motor race in Britain.
Up front: Italian cars in blood red.
Seventy laps later, an Italian named Giuseppe Farina wins.
Nobody watching knows it yet, but they've just seen the
first ever race of the Formula One World Championship.
But F1 didn't start that day.
It started fifty-six years earlier… with
a newspaper trying to sell more newspapers.
1894. Cars are brand new, noisy and unreliable.
Most people think they're a toy for rich weirdos.
So a Paris newspaper, Le Petit Journal, organises a challenge:
drive from Paris to Rouen, about 126 kilometres.
But it wasn't a race.
The prize was for the vehicle that was safe, easy to handle and cheap to run.
The fastest machine, a steam-powered one, didn't even get the top prize.
A year later came Paris–Bordeaux–Paris:
almost twelve hundred kilometres, there and back.
A man named Émile Levassor got back first,
after driving for about two days with almost no rest.
Why race at all? Because a race is the best advert there is.
If your car survives twelve hundred kilometres,
people believe it can survive their trip to the market.
That's reason number one F1 exists:
to prove the machine works.
Within a few years, cars got much faster.
The races didn't change.
They still ran on open public roads, between cities,
through dust, villages, and crowds standing right at the edge.
In 1903, more than two hundred cars set off from Paris to Madrid.
It turned into a disaster.
Crash after crash on the first day.
Drivers, mechanics and spectators were killed,
including Marcel Renault, one of the brothers who founded Renault.
The government stopped the race at Bordeaux.
The cars weren't even allowed to drive out under their own power.
After that, the era of racing between cities on open roads was basically over.
Racing moved onto closed circuits, loops of road closed to the public.
Reason number two: racing needed its own safe place, away from the public.
Around the same time, an American newspaper owner named James Gordon
Bennett set up a race between countries, not just car companies.
Every nation sent a team.
To tell them apart, each country got its own colour.
France raced in blue. Germany in white.
Italy in red.
Britain couldn't use red, white or blue:
those were taken. And in 1903, the British team raced in Ireland,
because racing on public roads was illegal in Britain.
So they picked green, in honour of Ireland's shamrock.
That's British racing green.
And that's why, more than a century later, Ferrari is still red.
It's Italy's old racing colour.
In 1906, the Automobile Club of France held
a new kind of race near the town of Le Mans.
They called it the Grand Prix:
French for "big prize".
The track was a loop of closed public roads,
more than a hundred kilometres around.
The race lasted two days, and covered over twelve hundred kilometres.
The winner was Ferenc Szisz, a Hungarian mechanic
driving for Renault, with a riding mechanic next to him.
Their average speed: about a hundred and one kilometres per hour.
On dirt roads. In 1906.
Grand Prix racing was born.
But it was still a mess.
Every race had its own rules, and there was no single champion.
In the 1930s, Grand Prix racing got a
European Championship, and it got political.
The German government poured money into two teams,
Mercedes-Benz and Auto Union, to show off German engineering.
Their cars were so dominant and so shiny
they became known as the "Silver Arrows".
There's a famous story that Mercedes scraped the white
paint off their car to make it light enough to race.
It's a great story. Historians say it's probably not true:
the weight limit wasn't even used at that race.
Then the Second World War stopped everything.
In Italy, Alfa Romeo had a small, brilliant racing car called the 158.
To keep it out of the war, the cars were hidden near Milan:
legend says in a cheese factory, other accounts say a pig farm.
Remember that car. It will be important.
After the war, the sport's governing body,
today called the FIA, wrote one rulebook for top-level racing:
a single "formula".
That's literally what the name means.
A formula is a set of rules every car must follow.
Engine size, weight, design.
Formula One was the top one.
Lower categories like Formula Two came later.
The first version allowed either big 4.5-litre engines,
or small 1.5-litre engines with a supercharger.
Why bother? Because without one formula,
the richest team just builds the biggest monster and wins.
A formula makes different machines race on roughly equal terms.
Reason number three: make it fair.
There was still one thing missing:
a single champion.
In 1949, motorcycles got their own world championship.
Car racing didn't want to be left behind.
So in early 1950, an Italian count named
Antonio Brivio suggested an idea at the FIA:
link the big national Grands Prix into one season,
give points to the top finishers, and crown one World Champion of drivers.
The first season had seven races:
six in Europe, plus the Indianapolis 500 in America,
which counted even though almost none of the European drivers went.
And the first race of all?
Silverstone. May 13th, 1950.
The car that won it was that same little Alfa Romeo 158,
the one that had spent the war hidden on a farm.
Giuseppe Farina won that day, and at the end of the season,
he became Formula One's first World Champion.
So why does Formula One exist?
Because people needed to prove their machines worked,
find a safe place to race them, make the fight fair, and crown one champion.
Seventy-six years later, it's the same four reasons.
Car makers still use F1 to prove their technology.
Teams still fight over the rulebook.
And twenty-something drivers still chase one title.
Not bad for a newspaper stunt.
If you want the next chapter:
how this sport went from a dangerous hobby
to a billion-dollar machine, subscribe.
See you on the grid.
